answers.reasoning: Hetty's innocent question ('shall Miss hear our spelling after, same as always?') reveals that the narrator, not the master, teaches; the room goes silent and Dask writes a line. No resentment, no comedy, and Hetty's knowledge is not the point.

Dask's ironic 'satisfactory under its present master' and coat remark lead the narrator to see she was 'only keeping a coat'; she puts it on and sits in the chair. Option 3 is mere summary; 0 overgeneralizes; 1 contradicts the text (Dask clearly noticed).
'six years of letters... all answered in a hand that had once been my brother's and was now mine' — she has imitated her dead brother's handwriting to the Ministry.

The Regulations require a certificated master; 'a woman might assist but not keep it' — yet she has kept the school well for six years. No dislike of teaching, wish to leave, or curate's demand appears.

'It wants wearing, Miss Penhallow, or the moth will have it' — the coat is the symbol of the master's role; Dask, addressing her by name, implies she should wear it/occupy the role rather than preserve it. The errand is set by the father ('Walk it for me'); the speaker carries his flask and map and plans to report back ('tonight I'll tell you'), so the 'you' makes the walk a report shaped for him. No resentment, no implication he is physically present.

The final stanza reframes the planned lie ('the keys are holding') as 'the kind a railway's made of: small, wooden, driven hard into the gap' — a track key that keeps the heavy thing from shifting, i.e., a supportive fiction. Not truth, not bitterness, not route-recording.

'in your chair at Fairholme, brakes on' suggests a wheelchair in a residence; 'a ganger's' pace identifies him as a former track gang worker. He is alive (she will speak to him tonight), not a station master or rambler.
Keys start as a literal task ('check the keys at Dunmore cutting') and end as the metaphor for the sustaining lie 'the keys are holding' — small fictions that hold things steady.
A wren 'goes off like a dropped spanner' conveys its sudden sharp sound, and the tool comparison ties the natural scene to the vanished railway labor.

Shoulder-high cow parsley shows overgrowth; a local dog-walker nods 'as if I'd come to read the meter' — the place is ordinary and casually used, not a heritage site, attraction, or dangerous wilderness.
'What you have lost is not the map. It's the walk' — he retains knowledge (he 'knew'); what he lacks is the ability to walk the eleven miles, a bodily loss rather than memory loss.

'Sleepers' puns on railway ties (just said to be gone) and the dozing father; 'still on the line' makes him the last remaining part of the dismantled track. He is not dead — she will speak with him tonight.

'small, wooden, driven hard into the gap to keep the heavy thing from shifting' describes a track key, the same object the father asked her to check; the lie is thus a humble part holding a heavy load.
'you knew. You pulled the last keys yourself' shows his memory is intact (no correction needed); 'So I finish it for you, at your pace' shows her walking in his stead, lending him her body.
Reader sees the original Portuguese sentence first, so when line 44 arrives the substitution is immediately recognizable; Dana, who doesn't speak Portuguese, hears only the revision.

Listing depositions, ERs, a miscarriage, and a drunk-driving plea in one even breath conveys professional flatness; the point is that the canon held through all of it. No mockery, grief, or doubt is voiced.
Agency dispatch, dry self-description as the only interpreter 'who will drive in snow'—a hired stranger with wry awareness of her usefulness.
She recalls the canon silently at the moment of hesitation, measuring the alteration she is about to make against the rule she has always kept.
'Eu sei' in Portuguese, after his 'that is not what I wrote,' is a private acknowledgment Dana cannot follow; she immediately asks 'What did he say?'
Trawlers frozen to moorings 'like plates left overnight in a sink'—stalled, idle, neglected.
The machine breathes for him with 'a small complaint, as if it, too, had been asked to work past its hours'—a weary laborer, mirroring prolonged dying.
The interpreter's merciful betrayal and the unnamed look on Aurelio's face leave the kindness's beneficiary ambiguous. Option 3 is summary, 0 and 1 overreach.

From folded arms to sitting on the bed and touching his knee—guarded daughter reaching toward father, prompted by the softened letter. 'Wholly forgiven' overreaches.

The boy wanted a grandfather who 'lied about the war over plum brandy' — a sociable tall-tale performance — rather than one who sat in silent, visible grief; 'lied' marks the comfortable fiction he'd have preferred.
'Glass on three sides, a timetable under glass' evokes transparency and scheduled arrivals, set against the old man's indefinite waiting on a weathered bench.
The tricolon 'at Easter, then at Christmas, then I meant to write' traces the letters dwindling to mere intention, in flat, unsparing parallel clauses.
Mornings he faced the eastern road (Pavel) publicly; afternoons, 'when the square had stopped watching,' he slid to the west arm facing the city road the speaker took — a private second vigil.
'Like a stopped clock' is the fourteen-year-old's judgment of uselessness ('I was ashamed of you'), later undercut when the speaker discovers the worn west arm.
'Twelve years I let you think the road was slow' admits the speaker, not the road, was the cause of the delay — he was the one who never came, making the poem a confession.
The speaker left on 'the western bus'; the arm 'that faces west, down the city road' worn smooth shows the grandfather also waited for him.
Argos, the dog who waited faithfully for Odysseus, emphasizes humble enduring loyalty; here the poignancy is that neither Pavel nor (in time) the speaker returns to reward it.
'I was then seventeen' and 'I have since learned' mark a retrospective adult narrator recalling his clerkship.
Boats 'like cattle that had given up', the Patience a 'long black scab', a net 'with no fish to keep' — the stranded, worn imagery mirrors Venn's life.
'as a man turns a coin he suspects' — the gesture signals distrust of the bargain.
He begins believing anything in a ledger can be understood; ends not opening his private book: 'figures... kept only by being left out.'
We see only through Pell, who judges Harrowby 'the coldest man in Skelwick' until the kitchen reveal corrects him; we share his error.
The delayed kitchen scene reverses our view of Harrowby's coldness and reframes Venn's refusal as a 'pleasure' the offer is designed to afford.
The housekeeper says the offer is made 'so that Venn may have the pleasure of refusing it', while Harrowby secretly overpays for his fish—pride and aid together.
'cattle that had given up' — working creatures lying down in tired resignation.
A drawer full of unsigned offers shows the proposal is renewed yearly and routinely declined—a ritual.
The 'only arithmetic' line reads as cold; the housekeeper's account reveals calculated, concealed kindness behind it.
'Everyone said so' frames the 'good's as the town's verdict; the stanza's soundness ('kept us in', thick walls) immediately turns into what the walls concealed, making the praise ironic.
Speaker taped boxes, rolled rugs, recalls father nailing boards in thirty-one, was eleven in the past, locks the house before sale: a grown daughter.

The turn at stanza 5 ('But I was the one') shifts from implicit accusation to confession; final refusal to look back ('raised better than that') ironically echoes the household's habit of not acknowledging.
The house 'heard' the voice; the child turned up the radio to cover it. The phrase registers the mother being diminished, perceived aurally not visually.
Stanza 4 has effectively accused the house of holding the abuse; after admitting she turned the radio up, she disclaims an accusation she has already largely made.
Radio turned up 'to cover it'; speaker herself 'knew the dial' and the loudest band—noise masking harm and her complicity.
The 'quiet' buyers praise is the same thick-walled silence that kept the abuse unheard; 'They'll mean it as a compliment' signals the irony.
Poem moves from describing the house's soundness and what it held to the speaker's own role in the silence and her final refusal to look back.
The ledger's 'Paid' with Pruitt's initials reveals the apparent unpaid account as quiet mercy toward a grieving widow; [0] overgeneralizes, [1] is summary, [3] contradicts the text.

Five stopped clocks, pendulum 'dead as a plumb line,' alongside the photo and flag: time halted by loss.
He rehearses a demand, then says 'No, ma'am'; the narrator gives no real reason, even admitting his excuse was false.
The demand becomes a coin held unspent in his mouth—the currency he believed the world ran on is now something he cannot use.
'In the winter of 1951 I was fifteen... I keep a shop of my own now.'
He supplies himself a false reason rather than confront the real one (grief, pity, unsettled faith in payment).
Penelope's weaving/unpicking parallels Mrs. Danner's winding and letting the watch stop—a ritual of waiting for a son who will not return.
The personified house strains to hear, mirroring the widow waiting for news; the stopped clocks and flag reinforce this.
The boy (and reader) believe the column is empty of payment until 'Paid' with Pruitt's initials recasts the account.
Photograph of a sailor boy and a folded flag nobody touches: a death kept present but unhandled.

The boy searches the ledger for figures; Pruitt's 'Paid' with his own initials shows the account as an obligation of care he settles himself.

Walt's own correction 'I was in pumps. For a while' recasts the present-tense claim as past and temporary; the other options overreach (suitcase/cash prove nothing; 'Pumps' is dry skepticism, not proof).
Opening the key drawer, not taking a key, closing it, then naming the kitchen room dramatizes her hesitation—weighing the concession physically before voicing it.

'Eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt' names him and reframes the twelve dollars as a tally of his absence, revealing she recognized him all along. It does not end the deal, demand full back pay, or inform him the bride is his daughter (he already seeks to see her).

Placing the key on the money rather than in his hand keeps the transaction commercial and avoids physical contact—shelter granted, intimacy/standing withheld. Fear, forgiveness, and pure profit motive are unsupported (she pockets the money in the apron with the hem pins, not the till).

The script withholds his name until Vera speaks it; the heading change aligns the audience's knowledge with the onstage unmasking. Option 2 wrongly claims the audience knew from the start; options 0 and 1 overstate his agency and trustworthiness.

She identifies him by a small habit—easing the door shut—described with precise, grudging memory ('You always did that'), showing intimate knowledge beneath resentment. Not admiration, not carelessness, not rehearsed waiting.
Having said he only wants to see her walk in and would stand outside, asking 'if I miss the bus?' hints at wanting to stay longer—more than a glimpse—without stating it.

'We're full' treats him as any stranger; 'Mind the door going up. The house is asleep' echoes his own door-closing habit and her earlier description of it, acknowledging him personally while still dismissing him to the back stairs and the morning bus.

The narrator insists she is 'never sentimental'; the ledger reveals the father's close attention to her, and her ending ('I find that I know all of them') admits the feeling only indirectly. Options 1-3 overreach or invert the text.
'A dealer does not pay more for clean glass' recasts leaving her father's things untouched as a purely commercial rationale, consistent with her claimed unsentimentality.
Pell's loud ticking watch in the silent room contrasts the running time of commerce with the shop's stopped, held hours; nothing suggests dishonesty or superior craft.
The pendulum held 'as a man holds his breath outside a sickroom' makes the shop seem to keep vigil over the father's death.
The childhood memory ('Hush, Nell'... 'It was always a clock') establishes her sense of being overlooked, which the ledger then overturns.
We see the father only through Nell's limited view, so the ledger's revelation surprises reader and narrator together.
She refuses to sell immediately after reading the ledger but frames it as 'a practical matter,' showing she has changed while refusing to name the emotion.
He claims never to wonder about passengers, yet notes her shoes, their resoling, and where she looks—attention his professed incuriosity can't explain.
Flat, tautological practicality that deflects any admission of interest.
'Color of weak tea' marks fading afternoon light after repeated crossings.
'A man could do worse than be a needle' is self-justification that ironically exposes a life without opinion or attachment.
'I wanted to see if it got easier... It doesn't. It only gets the same.'
The insistent denial ('I did not watch... There was no call to') betrays the feeling it denies.
We know only what Ostrander observes and chooses to tell.
He had moved the thermos onto the bench for her; returning it 'where it belongs' restores the prior order.
Operator since 1931 recounting October 1952 through March, in retrospect.
'A hem that never gets finished'—endless repetition without completion.
Reader knows the ninety-thousand figure, so his 'I didn't say' is recognized as evasion.

The seed is 'made for one thing, which is splitting,' yet release requires fire/war/drought; it calls itself 'a prayer that should not be answered' and asks forgiveness. Preservation forecloses living, and the wish to grow becomes a guilty wish for catastrophe. [0] ignores the longing, [1] overweights Teodor, [3] overgeneralizes.
'Down here... the underworld... At least they let her up for spring' casts the vault as an underworld; unlike Persephone, the seed has no promised seasonal return.
'They tell me minus eighteen is a kindness' reports an official claim at arm's length; the attribution to 'they' signals wry skepticism, not fury, confusion, or gratitude.
'Crack' puns on a seed cracking open to sprout and on cracking under strain; it fuses desire to grow with distress. No damage to the vault is reported and nothing is resolved.
'Twice a year the light comes on,' thick coat, roll call where 'nobody answers,' she 'goes out humming, and the dark shuts behind her' — cold, rarely visited, brief routine presence.
Dagny's rounds are impersonal and routine; Teodor's pencil note, licked flap, taste of salt and pipe smoke, talking to rows show intimate care the seed still feels. Neither is cruel or neglectful.
'I am a speckled bean... slept inside a foil envelope... for nine years'; it recalls Teodor and ends 'Forgive me, Teodor.' Still in the vault ('Down here').
'The mountain is patient. It has never wanted anything' contrasts with the seed's wanting ('I want it so badly'); the bank/coin simile makes its safety indifferent rather than loving or resentful.

'I can still taste him, salt and pipe smoke' shows intimate attachment; 'Forgive me, Teodor' shows guilt because its wish to grow depends on the world going wrong — something the farmer who said 'do not let them dry out' would not want.
The first-person seed lets the reader experience preservation as confinement ('holds us... never spent,' 'Down here'). No access to Dagny's thoughts, not objective, no detailed world news.

'I was made for one thing, which is splitting' (purpose) → 'what would open the door for good is fire, or a war, or the long drought' (cost) → 'So I am a prayer that should not be answered' (self-judgment).
'To be worth something, never spent' — like a banked coin, the seed's value depends on being held in reserve; valued and used are split apart, which is the poem's central irony.

Minus eighteen, 'envelope inside a box inside a mountain,' nine years of sleep — nested enclosures layer distance from the living, flooding field, making storage feel like burial (prepared for the underworld image later).
The tally becomes a ritual ('I keep the books,' 'Now I am thorough') that confirms she stays rather than goes; 'Not one of them has taken me.'
'She means it kindly' and her not asking about the marks show tactful restraint.
'Now' answers the brother's departure she 'did not count'; precision compensates for an earlier failure to notice.
'some parlor I will never sit in' stresses that even freight reaches lives she is excluded from.
The revelation 'That one I did not count' reframes the counting as a belated response to the unmarked departure.
A drawer opened and shut in the dark: brief domestic glimpse, offered then withdrawn.
The closing lines state directly that she counts to be sure 'that I am here,' not for those who leave.
Personification of the rails' sound as grievance, in keeping with the speaker's mood; no literal anger or neighbors.
The short line 'that I am here' isolates her presence as the fact the counting confirms.
'Keep the books' is an accounting metaphor; the uncounted departure is the debt she now makes up for.
The speaker knows the ticket's date is gone by and that no train has taken her; the reader sees Mrs. Pruett's misreading.
Room above a coal merchant's, wallpaper roses 'brown as tea,' and the landlady carrying a jug mark a modest, worn lodging.
She lodges, counts trains, keeps an expired ticket, and never goes; a lodger putting off her own journey.
